attack.final_span:
tense if I had instead expressed an offense taken.
A well-placed zinger is a powerful tool. It can immediately disarm an awkward, overly-signaling situation. Who doesn’t feel relaxed after an office jester makes fun of their mistake? In a meeting with a group that’s approaching my territory, I once used humor to let the group know that I intended to be “administering policy” rather than in a “selling” role. When I first learned about a critical hire who was not gender diverse, I inquired of the individual who was my immediate supervisor about it. He said, “You’ll like him.” Without even a moment to breathe I had responded: “You know me too well,” an awkward moment avoided.
Working on Wall Street, I learned about humor from the very top. I had the honor to sit opposite the renowned leader Jack Welch, who was frequently willing and able to laugh, whether at us or for laughs, and chuckles would immediately spread through the room as a consequence. I recall a particular meeting where the staff, dressed in their best clothes as representatives of sales, felt comfortable adding "telephone humor" to their repertoire, and shared an old favorite joke with Jack. He refused to be the butt of the joke. Yet with grace, he agreed to participate, choosing to overlook the joke and allow an assistant manager with a hangover to be considered for promotion in a scheme that went awry. When Jack witnessed Britney lose a struggle with a waiter, he recognized the straightforward reasons. He would often recall nervous meetings where it appeared an “officer caught with hookers” had damaged all the security guards’ cellphones, and Nixon and Kissinger had attended a political retreat. I would discuss with him the spam coming from abroad, and he would offer guidance akin to that of a former skeet shooting champion, one night consisting of randomly selecting pieces of missing wood from a gunsmith’s drawer. Success, in the end, wasn’t about technical mastery of functions. It was about making some folks laugh.
The Film Character Project’s report highlighted some distinctions between male and female characters.
Anthony F. Roberts, professor emeritus, Rutgers
